name: Tuvan kargyraa subharmonic throat-singing
lineage: Tuvan kargyraa subharmonic throat-singing tradition of the Republic of Tuva (southern Siberia, Russian Federation, bordering northwestern Mongolia). Kargyraa technique produces a fundamental pitched a full octave below the singer's normal speaking range through false-vocal-fold (ventricular) co-oscillation: the true vocal folds vibrate at one frequency while the ventricular folds vibrate at half that frequency, producing a rumbling subharmonic. Over this fundamental the singer shapes upper-partial overtone melodies. Two named regional variants: dag kargyraa ("mountain kargyraa," more open and resonant, associated with the Yenisei river valley) and khovu kargyraa ("steppe kargyraa," more compressed and growling, associated with the dry-steppe lowlands). Performance contexts span solo pastoral, hunters' contexts (the throat-singing reproducing animal-call and natural-sound mimesis), and contemporary international concert circuit. Often accompanied by igil (the two-string upright fiddle that is the Tuvan parallel to Mongolian morin khuur). Ted Levin's Where Rivers and Mountains Sing (Indiana UP 2006) is the principal English-language scholarly documentation; Zoya Kyrgys's The Mystery of Tuvan Khoomei (2002) the principal Tuvan-language reference; Smithsonian Folkways SFW40017 Tuva: Voices from the Center of Asia (1990, Levin/Hunt) the canonical Western-distributed recording. Distinguished from Mongolian kharkhiraa by Tuvan-Tyva dialect-specific technique nomenclature and characteristic dag-vs-khovu regional variants; distinguished from Tibetan yang chant by Tuvan kargyraa's solo-secular (vs ensemble-monastic-liturgical) framework; distinguished from sygyt by kargyraa's low-subharmonic (vs sygyt's high-overtone) register.
